name: Optic nerve, chiasm and tract
func: Carries vision from the eyes to the brain. At the optic chiasm, fibers from the inner half of each retina cross over, so each side of the brain sees the opposite half of the world.

levels.kid:
Your eyes are like two cameras, and the **optic nerves** are the cables that carry the pictures to your brain.

Each eye has its own cable. The two cables meet under the middle of your brain in a spot shaped like an **X**, called the **optic chiasm**. There, some wires cross over to the other side.

Because of that crossing, the left side of your brain looks at everything on your **right**, and the right side of your brain looks at everything on your **left**. Your brain then glues the two halves together, so you see one whole picture.
levels.hs:
The **optic nerve (cranial nerve II)** leaves the back of each eyeball and runs backward through the **optic canal** of the sphenoid bone into the skull. It is really a tract of the brain, not a true peripheral nerve, so it is wrapped in all three **meninges**.

The two optic nerves meet at the **optic chiasm**, which sits just above the **pituitary gland** and in front of the **pituitary stalk**, with the **hypothalamus** directly above and behind it. At the chiasm, fibers from the **nasal (inner) half** of each retina cross to the other side. Fibers from the **temporal (outer) half** stay on the same side.

After the chiasm, the fibers continue as the **optic tracts**, which wrap around the **cerebral peduncles** of the midbrain. Most end in the **lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN)** of the thalamus. From there, the **optic radiations** fan back to the **primary visual cortex** in the occipital lobe.

The result: the left optic tract carries everything you see in the **right visual field** from both eyes. Some fibers branch off to the midbrain for the **pupillary light reflex**, and others go to the hypothalamus to set your body clock.
levels.college:
About **1.2 million** retinal ganglion cell axons form each optic nerve. They gather at the **optic disc** (the blind spot) and become myelinated, by **oligodendrocytes**, only after passing through the **lamina cribrosa** of the sclera. The nerve has four parts: **intraocular**, **intraorbital** (about 25 mm, S-shaped to allow eye movement, inside the cone of eye muscles), **intracanalicular** (with the **ophthalmic artery** below it) and **intracranial**.

Relations matter clinically. The chiasm lies above the **diaphragma sellae** and the pituitary, below the **third ventricle** floor, between the two **internal carotid arteries**, and behind the **anterior communicating artery** complex. Most people have a "central" chiasm directly over the sella, but some have a **prefixed** or **postfixed** chiasm.

Inferior nasal fibers crossing in the chiasm were classically said to loop forward into the opposite optic nerve (**Wilbrand's knee**), but later studies suggest the knee may be an artifact; this is debated.

The **optic tract** carries crossed and uncrossed fibers to the **LGN**, which has six layers: layers 1 and 2 are **magnocellular** (motion), layers 3–6 are **parvocellular** (detail and color). Crossed fibers end in layers 1, 4 and 6; uncrossed in 2, 3 and 5. Some tract fibers go to the **pretectal nuclei** (light reflex), the **superior colliculus** (orienting) and the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** (circadian rhythm).

The **optic radiations** split: the lower retina fibers loop forward through the temporal lobe (**Meyer's loop**), while upper retina fibers run through the parietal lobe.
levels.phd:
Retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) come in more than 40 molecularly defined types in mice, each tiling the retina and computing a distinct feature (ON/OFF, direction selectivity, edges). In primates the dominant classes are **midget** (parvocellular, high acuity, red–green opponency) and **parasol** (magnocellular, motion and contrast), plus **small bistratified** cells feeding the **koniocellular** layers (blue–yellow).

**Intrinsically photosensitive RGCs (ipRGCs)** contain **melanopsin** and respond directly to light, especially blue wavelengths. They project via the **retinohypothalamic tract** to the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**, setting the circadian clock, and to the **olivary pretectal nucleus**, driving sustained pupillary constriction. That is why some people with rod–cone blindness still entrain to light.

Decussation is set in development. At the chiasm midline, radial glia express **ephrin-B2**; RGCs from the ventrotemporal retina express **EphB1** (controlled by the transcription factor **Zic2**) and are repelled, so they stay ipsilateral. In albinism, reduced melanin alters this decision and too many fibers cross, disrupting binocular vision.

The optic nerve is a CNS tract and does not regenerate after injury, a classic model for axon regeneration research. Deleting **PTEN** or **SOCS3**, or enhancing mTOR signaling, lets some RGC axons regrow in mice, and a few reach the brain. **Hemidecussation** creates a precise retinotopic map in the LGN and in **V1**, where left and right eye inputs remain segregated into **ocular dominance columns** (Hubel and Wiesel), shaped by activity during a **critical period**.
levels.expert:
Visual field defects localize the lesion precisely:
- **Optic nerve**: monocular vision loss, a **relative afferent pupillary defect** (swinging flashlight test), reduced color vision and, later, optic atrophy.
- **Chiasm**: **bitemporal hemianopia**, classically from a **pituitary macroadenoma** pressing up from below (upper fields go first). **Craniopharyngioma** in children and suprasellar meningiomas press from above.
- **Optic tract**: **incongruous homonymous hemianopia**.
- **Meyer's loop** (temporal lobe): contralateral superior quadrantanopia, "pie in the sky," a risk in temporal lobe epilepsy surgery.
- **Parietal radiations**: inferior quadrantanopia.
- **Occipital cortex** (often a PCA stroke): congruous homonymous hemianopia with **macular sparing**.
- A **junctional scotoma** (central loss in one eye plus a superior temporal defect in the other) points to a lesion where an optic nerve meets the chiasm.

**Optic neuritis** causes painful vision loss in young adults and is linked to **multiple sclerosis**, MOG antibody disease and **NMOSD** (aquaporin-4 antibodies). **Papilledema** is optic disc swelling from raised intracranial pressure. **Ischemic optic neuropathy** and **glaucoma** damage the nerve head.

**MRI with contrast** through the sella and orbits is key; formal **perimetry** charts the fields. Pituitary tumors compressing the chiasm are usually removed by an **endoscopic endonasal transsphenoidal** approach, often with rapid visual recovery; some hormone-secreting adenomas are treated with medication first. **Optic nerve gliomas** occur in children with **neurofibromatosis type 1**. The **optic nerve sheath** can be fenestrated in selected cases of raised pressure.

keyPoints: Optic nerve → chiasm (above the pituitary) → optic tract → LGN → optic radiations → occipital cortex
Nasal retinal fibers cross at the chiasm; temporal fibers stay on the same side
Each hemisphere sees the opposite visual field
Meyer's loop lesion → 'pie in the sky' superior quadrantanopia

test.q: A pituitary macroadenoma compressing the optic chiasm classically causes:
test.explain: Crossing nasal fibers, which see the temporal fields, are compressed at the chiasm.

test.q: Retinal fibers from which half of each retina cross at the chiasm?
test.explain: Nasal fibers cross; temporal fibers stay ipsilateral.

test.q: Most optic tract fibers synapse in the:
test.explain: The LGN of the thalamus relays to V1 via the optic radiations.

test.q: A temporal lobe lesion affecting Meyer's loop produces:
test.explain: Meyer's loop carries lower retinal fibers, which see the upper visual field: 'pie in the sky.'

test.q: The light-sensitive pigment in ipRGCs that sets the body clock is ______.
test.explain: Melanopsin ipRGCs project to the suprachiasmatic nucleus and pretectum.
